title: Breaking And Entering: Ripple Effect Band On The Importance Of Storytelling
summary: Ripple Effect Band members Jodie Kell and Rachel Thomas stopped by the studio to talk with Lauren and Simon about songwriting in the now-endangered language of their people, their home on Arnhem Land and how they came to be the critically acclaimed all woman rock band.
transcript:
Rachel Thomas and Jodie Kell of Ripple Effect Band joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 1 May 2025, the day after the band performed at the APRA Music Awards. They discussed their debut album Mayawa, the band's beginnings in Maningrida, and the connections between language, country and song. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: As Lauren mentioned, it's such a huge honour and a thrill to have you with us today. For listeners who haven't encountered your music so regularly, a little introduction: Ripple Effect Band are a groundbreaking group in so many ways, from the remote community of Maningrida in West Arnhem Land, in the Northern Territory. You're the first women from your community to form a band, with a very distinctive sound that's been described as saltwater rock, blending reggae and blues, and deeply rooted in your connection to country. A central tenet of your work is the use of multiple languages, including the highly endangered Na-kara, so the music is not only a beautiful source of enrichment but also an act of cultural preservation and revitalisation. And you were playing the APRA Awards last night. We saw some great videos, including, I think, your cover of King Stingray's 'Through The Trees'. Can you tell us about your experience last night?

Rachel: It was good last night, and there were too many at the front. But it's difficult. They're different to us. They're from East Arnhem.

Simon: It would have been an extraordinary experience. There are so many beautiful stories you're sharing and important themes you're exploring, and in a live music context it's quite special as well. What do you hope people feel or take away when they see you perform?

Jodie: We love performing live and sharing the music, and I think there's something special about seeing the women playing the instruments and singing live. Last night, like Rachel was saying, King Stingray are from East Arnhem, and also they're men. The women are from West Arnhem, and women. So we switched things around in the middle section, when they sing what they call manikay or bunggul, traditional song. We can't sing that as women. Rachel had a beautiful song that she'd written, which was about the sunset.

Rachel: It's all about the story that I'm sitting up the cliff and watching the sun going down. I turn around and look at the rain coming toward us, and in the ocean I can see the lightning striking. So it's all about my language.

Jodie: It's got a traditional kun-borrk feeling to it. It's different but the same. A lot of people last night afterwards were saying they could feel this deep meaning in the music because of the way we were performing. It meant a lot to all of us to have that chance to sing that big band King Stingray's song, but change it up, and show respect to East Arnhem and show respect to West Arnhem: the connections, and yet the difference as well.

Lauren: We'd love to go back to the start. How did Ripple Effect Band first come together?

Rachel: What a long time ago, when we were young ladies.

Jodie: I went to Maningrida in 2000 as a schoolteacher, teaching music in the high school. That was when the girls started learning, because there was myself, and there was Zeb Olsen, who's up in Castlemaine, and also Megan Atfield. So having women teachers was big. For me personally, a really important thing was that I would sit on the front veranda of my house and hear this beautiful singing coming from next door. I'd only just moved there, and I got braver and braver, and one day I walked around the fence and there was this lady and her husband, very young and skinny. That was Rachel and her husband, singing beautiful gospel and also history songs like 'Makéddja', Turtle Song, Hunting Song.

Rachel: She heard us, me and my partner. We were singing. It's a cliff song. We were both sitting there, watching the island, and she heard us. She came there to sit with us, myself and my partner.

Jodie: They opened their arms. I said, 'I want to learn,' and they just taught me everything. That was the beginning of a big friendship and music together. If you listen to our single of 'Walaya', not the one on the album but the single we released, at the very beginning there's a recording done on a tape player of Rachel's partner singing that song. He's passed away now, so that's a tribute to him and that beautiful moment.

Simon: There are beautiful tributes to family and community throughout the debut album, Mayawa, released last year. Perhaps we could talk about one in particular, Rachel: the story of Cyclone Monica, which we understand includes your mother's voice as part of the recording. Could you share the significance of this story, and what it was like recording it?

Rachel: My mum, she used to tell all about spirit dreaming. It's called Djómi. People come from other places, she go out to the barge landing or in the sacred site to start calling out for the Djómi, spirit Djómi. So she can sing out and they will look after them, those people.

Lauren: We understand the album's title, Mayawa, translates as beach, or coast, in Na-kara, and there are lots of stories relating to this region. How does the name reflect the spirit of the album?

Jodie: We spend a lot of time at the beach. We love fishing and hunting. Maningrida is on the coast, on the mouth of the Liverpool River. When you head out of town on the dirt road, you can head towards Darwin, or you take a left, and then you go along there and you can go to all these places like Makórrdja, Ndjúdda. Makórrdja looks back to Maningrida, and then you come around the point to Ndjúdda, which is beautiful.

Rachel: It goes round and round, from Nardilmuk to Ndjúdda, Makórrdja. And the other way, keep going, Nardilmuk to Rocky Point. Berraja, all the way.

Jodie: We spend a lot of time along there. You might go, 'Let's go to Rocky Point. We'll go to dinner camp, we'll go fishing there,' or, 'Let's go to Ndjúdda, get some wengala,' or Makórrdja to get crab. There's lots of crab.

We don't go to the beach and lie around. There's too much to do. It's a time when you're out and you're hunting, and we sit around the fire and we sing songs and we think about all the old people and all the history, and tell stories. In naming the album, we spoke with Rona and her grandmother, and we said we'd like to name it for those times spent out on the country.

Simon: Ripple Effect Band sing in multiple languages, especially the endangered Na-kara language we were speaking about earlier, and that's been very central to your identity. Can you tell us about the importance of weaving language through song?

Rachel: We speak Ndjébbana.

Jodie: So the Ndjébbana language that Rachel speaks is connected to the country. When you sing about country, you sing in language.

Rachel: We sing Ndjébbana, we sing Na-kara, we sing Burarra and Kune. Kune is inland, so that's freshwater country. We are the saltwater country.

Jodie: When we sing, say, 'Cyclone', because 'Cyclone' is about Maningrida, which is the Dhukurrdji clan, Dhukurrdji land, part of the Ndjébbana language group, you sing in that language. Then when you sing 'Na-meyarra', which is about Na-kara land, you sing in that language. So the language connects to the country, and it connects to the stories.

Lauren: The band's name itself carries that idea of influence and impact. What effects of your music are you seeing on the community in Maningrida and beyond?

Jodie: When I was in Maningrida just around Easter, I saw the school bus going past, and they were playing 'Na-kalamandjarda' out of the school bus. It's important for all the children. They love singing, and they love singing in language. With the 'Cyclone' song, we worked with a big school event in Sydney, so 400 schoolchildren sang 'Cyclone' at the Sydney Opera House, with a string ensemble and piano. It was so exciting that the school then organised for the whole school to sing the same version, with the recorded violins. Rachel was there, and all the mob were there too, like David Jones and the traditional landowners. What were they doing? Did they like it?

Rachel: My auntie, she loved that Monica Cyclone song.

Lauren: How did it feel for you to see?

Rachel: It also reminds me about my mum, because she knows all the Djómi spirit running away and then still coming back again. I'm really proud for my song about Monica Cyclone, from where I come from, Maningrida, called Dhukurrdji.

Simon: We've lined up a special version of 'Cyclone' that you recorded live for us at Triple R, in the performance space towards the end of last year. Are you working on new material? What's next for Ripple Effect Band?

Jodie: Seeing that we love Triple R so much, I might just say there may be a single coming out soon. We haven't fully announced it yet, but keep your ears posted; of course we'll let you all know. We did a bit of recording in Castlemaine last year while we were down. Then we've got ideas for a new album. We've been singing lots of different songs, thinking about Patricia's new song, 'Hunting Song'. We have one that we've been thinking about, about all the travelling we do and all the different places we go and share music, and how fun that is. So I reckon a new album is in the works, but definitely a new song. There you go, I've said it now. Surprise.

Lauren: We cannot wait. Rachel and Jodie from Ripple Effect Band, thank you so much for joining us on Breaking and Entering today.
